div.p: In the early phases of embedded real-time systems development, design decisions are made with large consequences on the quality of the resulting product. At the same time, only limited information is available about key attributes, which makes it difficult to get correct decisions. In this paper, it is studied how to include uncertainty in the information in early phases and to handle the risks involved. Using Monte Carlo simulation, the uncertainties are evaluated based on estimations of basic parameters. The technique is applied to schedulability analysis, and it is shown that the results can be counter-intuitive, and thus that current design practice can lead to higher risk than assumed by the designers.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: When a new technical system is developed, the early design phases are always critical. In those phases, the basic concepts are selected, and they effectively limit what can be achieved in the subsequent stages in terms of, e.g., cost and performance. But the early phases are characterized by a lack of information, and of ad hoc decisions based on the intuition and experience of the engineers. It seems natural to try to improve the early phases by providing methods that give better indications of the important attributes of the system, and that quantify the risks. Far-reaching redesigns late in the project can then be avoided, thus reducing the cost, duration, and risk of development.

For embedded real-time systems (ERTS), the important conceptual design decisions involve selecting the hardware architecture, and the distribution of functionality. The ability of the ERTS to meet its timing constraints is thus to a great extent fixed very early on. Still, much of the research in the area has focused on how to verify that the timing constraints are met in the end, whereas much less work exists on how to ensure that the right decisions are made in the first place, and virtually nothing has been done on establishing the risk of performance problems early in the project which is somewhat surprising when considering the practical importance of that topic.

The research question in the paper is whether an explicit modeling of uncertainties can improve design decisions in the early phases. The main contribution is an analysis method based on Monte Carlo simulations, where attributes are stated as probability distributions rather than point values, to capture the uncertainties. The method is applied to ERTS design, focusing on the system's ability to reach its timing constraints. It is shown that this provides valuable additional information, and gives a clearer indication of the risk associated with a design. The results are to some extent counter-intuitive, which further emphasizes the fact that the methodology provides an added value compared to the current practice of having experienced engineers do estimations based on their intuitive understanding.

In the next section, the characteristics of the early phases of ERTS design are described. In Section 3, estimations are discussed, and some difficulties are identified. In Section 4, Monte Carlo simulation is introduced, and the technique is applied to an example application focusing on an early assessment of schedulability. Finally, the conclusions are presented.

div.head: Early phases of ERTS design
div.p: In this section, we discuss some characteristics of the early conceptual phases of ERTS design.

div.head: Early design decisions
div.p: In the early phases, it is usually necessary to make overall decisions about the parts, such as what electronic control units (ECUs) should be present in the network, what processors to use and what memory capacity is needed. These decisions can in practice hardly be delayed since they affect the overall product and the project plan. They provide input for activities such as software development, packaging of ECUs in the product, environmental requirements (e.g., temperature, vibrations, EMC) for ECU detailed design, and investment in tooling for mass production.

In the early phases, the detailed functionality is unknown, including task deadlines and periods, since these are derived from the overall closed-loop behavior of the embedded system in its physical environment, which is being developed in parallel with the ERTS. The set of tasks that implement the functions is also preliminary, with only estimates of execution time.

The early design decisions that have a large impact on the ERTS's ability to reach its deadlines, including the choice of hardware architecture, are thus made based on rough estimates of key parameters such as execution time, deadlines, and periods. The estimations are typically point values, that do not provide any indication of the uncertainty. This makes it difficult to reason about the risk associated with a particular design alternative, and to systematically compare different alternatives. There are also large variations in the knowledge about different parts of the new system. For components that already exist in previous products, many attributes are well known, and can be measured, and the software code could even exist, but for new parts knowledge is scarce. This means that a realistic estimation approach for early phases must be able to handle such discrepancies in the available knowledge.

div.head: Schedulability analysis
div.p: When a system is developed, the goal is to ensure that it meets its final verification tests, and for an ERTS such a test is to ensure that all tasks are schedulable. The actual schedulability test used depends on what principle is chosen for the scheduler, and the method presented in this paper should work with most scheduling policies. As an example, we will apply it to a standard pre-emptive fixed-priority scheduler. The system thus consists of a set of tasks {τ 1 , ..., τ n } executed on a single processor. C i denotes the maximum execution time of τ i , D i is the deadline of τ i , and T i is the period of τ i , where D i ≤ T i . Configuring the scheduler consists of assigning priorities to the tasks.

div.head: Minimal required speedup
div.p: The outcome of a classical schedulability analysis is binary, a "yes" or a "no", depending on whether all tasks meet their deadlines or not. However, in many cases it is useful to have a continuous metric that states how well the timing constraints are met. For instance, when two alternative designs are evaluated in the early phases, it might be desirable to know which one of them has a larger margin in terms of spare capacity. In practice, designers may use metrics such as processor load to get a feeling for how large the margins are, but this may be grossly misleading, as will be seen below.

In [2], a schedulability metric called minimal required speedup (MRS) is introduced. It is defined as the factor by which a system would have to be accelerated (or decelerated) to exactly meet the deadlines. Intuitively, if the system runs at a certain clock speed, MRS says how much faster (or slower) the clock speed would have to be to exactly meet all deadlines. If MRS ≤ 1, all deadlines are met, and if MRS > 1, some deadlines are not fulfilled. The metric thus provides more insight into the characteristics of the system than a simple binary answer. It can also be used for any ERTS, regardless of the hardware or scheduling mechanism, or whether the system is distributed or not. For the fixed-priority scheduler, the MRS is the smallest factor S, such that if all C i are divided by S the system will meet all deadlines.

div.head: Estimations in the early phases
div.p: We will now discuss estimations in the early phases and determine a suitable probability distribution to capture the uncertainty of the estimation.

div.head: Estimations
div.p: The basic methodology followed when doing estimations of key attributes in the early phases is: 1. Identify attributes needed for the design decisions. 2. Create a model that links those attributes to other attributes at a lower level of design. 3. Estimate the values for the lower level attributes including uncertainty.

For ERTS, a critical attribute is the schedulability, captured by MRS. The model in the second step could be the same that will be used to verify schedulability. For fixed-priority scheduling, the lower level attributes are worst case execution time, deadline, and period.

Once the lower level attributes are identified, the designers can estimate them based on their best knowledge. By describing the attributes as probability distributions, they can capture the uncertainty by assessing some key points, such as the 50 th and 90 th percentile (i.e., the values that the person believes the attribute will, by 50% or 90% certainty, not exceed).

div.head: Weibull distribution
div.p: In some cases it is reasonable to assume that estimations follow the Gaussian distribution, but for practical applications the range is often limited in one end. Examples of this is time, cost, weight, temperature (in Kelvin), and physical size. For such parameters, a normal distribution would always assign a certain probability to impossible negative values.

An alternative is to use a distribution which gives zero probability to all negative values. In [4], a number of such distributions are discussed for the purpose of cost estimation, and the authors conclude that the Weibull distribution is suitable. div.head: Monte Carlo-based evaluation
div.p: In this section, a brief overview of Monte Carlo simulations is given. It is based on the steps described in Section 3.1. A number of iterations is run, each consisting of the following steps: 1. Generate random values for the low level attributes, according to their probability distributions.

div.head: Put those values into the evaluation model that links
div.p: the low level attributes to the high level ones.

div.head: Collect the outputs from the model in a histogram
div.p: for each high level attribute. The histograms will after the completed simulation show the probability distributions for the high level attributes, and can be used to determine key information such as mean values and the confidence that the critical parameters will have acceptable values.

The Monte Carlo simulation is very general and assumes almost nothing about the evaluation model, which can be an existing piece of software. It does not require any cumbersome analytical application of probability theory, and allows parameters with varying distributions corresponding to different levels of knowledge as described in Section 2.1.

div.head: Point value analysis
div.p: As a first step, we analyze the example based on exact values. This corresponds to the analysis done when verifying the completed system, but could also be done if the attributes were estimated values, in which case the uncertainty of the result would be unknown.
According to deadline monotonic scheduling [1],

the optimal priority assignment for this task set is τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 4 , and τ 3 , in descending priority order. All tasks meet their deadlines; hence the outcome of the schedulability analysis is "yes". However, this answer alone does not really indicate how large the margin is in the system. If the designer does a load analysis, it will turn out that the processor load is 50%, which could give the impression that the margins are large. However, if the MRS is calculated, it turns out that it is equal to 1, since τ 3 will exactly meet its deadline after the critical instant, thus there is actually no margin at all. The MRS thus provides valuable additional information compared to traditional schedulability analysis.

div.head: Defining the model
div.p: In the next step, a model is created for the Monte Carlo simulation. We chose to estimate the attributes using a Weibull distribution with α = 2, since that gives a shape that corresponds to the intuitive understanding of how estimations for these parameter look. As the 50 th percentile, we take the point value for each parameter in the original problem formulation, and as the 90 th percentile, we assume consistently a 50% higher value.

Since the deadline must never exceed the period, we estimate T i -D i instead of T i directly and calculate the actual period from that estimation and the estimation of D i . For those tasks where the deadline equals the period in the original problem a constant probability distribution of 0 is used for T i -D i . This gives the attributes provided in Table 2, from which the parameters of the Weibull distribution are easily fitted.

It should be emphasized that the probability distribution for C i does not model how the execution time varies between different activations of a task, but it captures the uncertainty in the estimation of worst case execution time. Based on the data in Table 2, we executed the Monte Carlo simulation with 10 000 iterations. The priority assignment needs to be redone in each iteration to ensure optimal schedulability.

div.head: Analyzing the results
div.p: Based on the Monte Carlo simulation, we collect data on MRS for all tasks and for the system as a whole. Figure 1 shows the overall MRS, and as can be seen the curve has its peak around the value 1, which is what would be expected since the MRS of the mean values is exactly 1. However, a more careful analysis of the data shows that the probability of having MRS ≤ 1 is actually only about 35%, which must be regarded as a very high risk to the project. Compared to the traditional schedulability and load analysis discussed above, this poor result would probably be regarded as counter-intuitive by many engineers, who would believe that the system had much better odds for reaching the deadlines. If a calculation based on mean values gives an MRS of exactly 1, intuition would lead one to believe that calculations based on probability distributions would give about 50% chance to meet the deadlines. In fact, the 50 th percentile is at MRS ≈ 1.22, and the 90 th percentile is at MRS ≈ 1.68, which is very far from reaching the deadlines.

Another aspect of interest is how priorities were assigned in the simulations, and this is shown in Table 3. This is as expected, since it follows the mean values for the estimated deadlines, and there are essentially two groups, with τ 1 and τ 2 getting priority 1 and 2, and τ 3 and τ 4 getting priority 3 and 4 in almost all cases. One of the strengths of fixed priority scheduling is that the actual priority assignment can be decided very late in the project. However, if that were not the case, this information would have been very valuable, since it shows that a priority assignment can be done early on without large implications on the overall system. There are many other attributes in practical ERTS for which such an analysis would be useful.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we have presented a methodology for explicitly dealing with uncertainties in the early phases of developing ERTS, with focus on the temporal attributes. Many industrial projects struggle with performance problems late in the development, leading to extra cost and delays due to redesigns. Our analysis shows that such problems could actually be discovered much earlier if proper methods were employed. The methodology presented is easy to use, and very flexible, so that no special requirements are put on the system or tools.
